title: Portfolio & mathematics library
intro: A personal workspace for my research, development and teaching, with a growing mathematics library at its heart.

brief: Bring different kinds of work together without making every page look or behave the same. The portfolio introduces the person; the library gives students a focused place to read, understand and practise.
context: An ongoing personal project. One unit is available in each of Classes 9 and 10; Classes 11 and 12 are planned.

decisions.title: A shared visual language
decisions.text: Typography, colour, navigation and controls carry across the portfolio and books. Reading views keep their own measure, while Practice papers have a separate printable layout.

decisions.title: Content with a source of truth
decisions.text: Authored pages, mathematical content and question banks are separate from shared components. The static build generates the public site, and checks run before publication.

reflection: An attractive page is only part of the job. The work also involves complete mathematical explanations, dependable navigation, responsive controls and repeatable publication.
next: Expand the books with independent mathematical review, recover a maintainable authoring path for Class 9, and continue consolidating the shared reading and Practice tools.

title: Omnifood
intro: A responsive landing page for a fictional food subscription service. A study in visual hierarchy, page rhythm and adapting content to different screens.

views.label: Desktop
views.caption: Desktop presentation: the introduction leads into the service, meals and pricing.

views.label: Tablet
views.caption: Tablet presentation: the same page adapts to a narrower reading space.

views.label: Mobile
views.caption: Mobile presentation: a single-column view of the original learning project.

brief: Give a visitor a clear route from understanding the service to exploring meals, plans and the sign-up form. Photography and section hierarchy need to work together across a long page.
context: Built through Jonas Schmedtmann’s HTML and CSS course. Omnifood is a fictional brand, not a client commission.

decisions.title: An order for the information
decisions.text: The introduction establishes the service before the page moves into meal examples, social proof and pricing. Each section answers a different question rather than repeating the same sales message.

decisions.title: Layouts that rearrange
decisions.text: Columns, images, navigation and the form adapt to the available width. The device views make these layout changes visible without requiring the visitor to resize their own browser.

reflection: A responsive page depends on more than smaller type. Image proportions, line lengths, navigation and the order of information all affect whether the page remains clear.
nextTitle: Where I would take it next
next: Revisit the original implementation with keyboard and assistive-technology testing, tighter asset delivery and real content. Any claims about usability or conversion would need evidence from actual users.

title: Animated sign-in interface
intro: Two forms, one shared composition. An exploration of how layout and coordinated motion can connect sign-in and registration.

views.label: Desktop
views.caption: Desktop presentation: forms and the coloured panel share one composition.

views.label: Tablet
views.caption: Tablet presentation: registration within the same visual system.

views.label: Mobile
views.caption: Mobile presentation: the original compact arrangement of the form and panel.

brief: Make switching between sign-in and registration feel like a change of state within one interface. Keep the form hierarchy clear while the surrounding panel changes position.
context: A frontend learning prototype. The public demo shows interface behaviour; it does not provide a working authentication service.

decisions.title: One state, coordinated motion
decisions.text: A class on the main container controls the visual state. CSS positions the forms and coloured panel, while JavaScript switches that state in response to the controls.

decisions.title: Keep the task recognisable
decisions.text: Fields, the main action and the option to switch forms retain a clear grouping. The saved device views show how the composition was arranged for different screen sizes.

reflection: Small interfaces make timing and hierarchy very noticeable. Several moving elements need a common state, and motion must never make the form harder to understand or use.
next: A production version needs secure server-side authentication, proper field labels and errors, password-manager support, keyboard testing and a reduced-motion option. Those are separate from the visual prototype.

title: The Pig Game
intro: A two-player dice game about when to keep rolling and when to hold. A compact exercise in connecting rules, state and visual feedback.

views.label: Gameplay
views.alt: The Pig Game showing the two player panels and game controls
views.caption: Original gameplay view. Try the demo to explore rolling, holding and restarting.

brief: Translate a turn-based game into a dependable interface. The current player, temporary score and accumulated scores must stay in agreement with every roll, hold and restart.
context: A JavaScript learning project. The gallery preserves the original gameplay image; additional device captures are not available.

decisions.title: Explicit state changes
decisions.text: Rolling changes the turn score, holding banks it, and restarting returns the game to its initial state. Keeping those operations distinct makes the rules easier to follow in the code.

decisions.title: Make the turn visible
decisions.text: The active-player treatment, die image and score displays give immediate feedback. A player can see both what changed and whose decision comes next.

reflection: A small game is a useful test of event handling and conditional logic. The screen must reflect the current state after every action, including the end of a game and a fresh start.
next: Add explicit tests for turn changes, score resets and winning states, then revisit keyboard access and small-screen play. The original demo remains available as a record of the learning project.
